idiom_name: enum Phase { ... } + match in the context method
implementation_notes: The Rust book's more natural encoding: states are variants of one enum (each carrying its own data), the machine is a struct holding that enum, and behaviour is selected with match, which the compiler requires to be exhaustive so a newly added state cannot be forgotten. Transitions are ordinary value assignments, there is no allocation and no dynamic dispatch, and the state compares and serializes naturally. This replaces the trait-object hierarchy for closed state sets; reach for trait objects only when states must be extensible outside the crate.
pitfalls: An exhaustive match only holds while the enum is closed to your crate; a #[non_exhaustive] enum forces a wildcard arm and loses the guarantee.
Matching by value moves the state out; match on &self.phase or make the enum Copy when the previous state must stay readable.
Closing the state set in an enum means downstream extensibility must be designed in advance or delegated to a trait object.

variants.name: Trait objects with Box<dyn State>
variants.idiom_name: struct Post { state: Option<Box<dyn State>> } with take() on transition
variants.implementation_notes: The book's first, object-oriented form: a private State trait, one struct per state, and Box<dyn State> in the context. Rust forces two adjustments: the field is Option<Box<dyn State>> because a transition consumes the current state (self: Box<Self>) and must take() it out before installing the successor, and every transitioning method needs &mut self. Choose this form when the state set is open (states supplied by other crates) or when a state owns trait objects itself; the enum form is cheaper and checked for exhaustiveness otherwise.
pitfalls: take() leaves the state as None for the duration of the transition; keep take-and-install in a single statement so a panic cannot leave the object stateless.
Box<dyn State> needs Send/Sync bounds for cross-thread use and 'static for safe ownership of state data.
Dynamic dispatch plus one allocation per transition costs more than the enum form and hides the state set from exhaustiveness checking.
